name: QR Barcode Art
basis: machine-readable code layout filled by ordered dither (how)

lumenary.blurb: Your picture as a QR-style square of black modules, or as the bar widths of a barcode.

facts.bestOn: Bold, high contrast pictures and logos

why: A QR code looks like noise but follows strict structure: three large squares in the corners, a smaller alignment square and alternating timing lines. This treatment copies that structure so the picture looks like a code at a glance, then fills the free cells from the photograph. It will not scan, but it keeps the visual language of a machine-readable label.
how: Lay out the three finder squares, the alignment square and the timing lines.
Measure brightness for every other module.
Add a Bayer threshold to it and make the module black when the result is below a half, which is an ordered dither.
In bar mode, stack thin bands and place bars at fixed spacing along each one.
Make each bar’s width follow the darkness of the picture, and print a row of digits beneath.
history: The barcode was patented by Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver in 1952, and the first product was scanned in a supermarket in 1974. The QR code was created in 1994 by Masahiro Hara at Denso Wave to track car parts in Japan, and it became everyday with smartphone cameras. Real codes use error correction, so part of the code can be damaged and still scan.
terms: One small square of a QR code.
The large square in a corner that lets a scanner locate and orient the code.
Turning grey into black and white dots using a repeating threshold pattern.
paragraphs: A QR code is a square of black and white modules with three large squares in the corners that tell a scanner where it is. This treatment keeps those finder patterns, a smaller alignment pattern and the alternating timing lines, so it looks like a code at a glance, and fills every other module from the picture. A module is black when the picture’s brightness there, shifted by a Bayer threshold, is below a half. The shifted threshold is an ordered dither, so mid-greys come out as a regular mix of black and white. It is not a working code and will not scan.

In barcode mode the picture is a stack of thin bands. In each band the bars are placed at a fixed spacing along the width, and the width of each bar follows the darkness of the picture at that point, so dark places have thick bars and light places thin ones. A row of digits is printed under it.

equations.note: The 7 × 7 finder pattern: a ring, a gap and a centre block.
Ink when the brightness plus a Bayer offset is below a half.
Bar width in barcode mode, for a unit width u.

presets.text: High detail with round modules softens the grid.
White on black is a night version.
Switch to bars for a barcode portrait.
